lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The Prophet's early life and the Revelation (spec 1.1-1.2)
lessons.title: 1.1 The Prophet's ancestry and early years
objectives: Outline the Prophet's ancestry and main events from birth to youth
Explain the roles of Halimah, Abdul Muttalib, Abu Talib and Bahira
Explain how his early life prepared him for prophethood

keywords.def: the leading tribe of Makkah to which the Prophet belonged
the clan of the Prophet within Quraysh
a monk of Busra who recognised signs of prophethood
an orphan

starter: Write one fact about the Year of the Elephant (Surah 105).
Who was the Prophet's mother and father?
State what 'seerah' means and why it is studied.

teach.heading: Ancestry and birth
bullets: Descended from Ibrahim through Isma'il
Tribe: Quraysh; clan: Banu Hashim
Born in Makkah around 570 CE, the Year of the Elephant
Father Abdullah died before his birth
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and salawat. Muslim records the Prophet's saying that Allah chose Kinanah from the sons of Isma'il, Quraysh from Kinanah, Banu Hashim from Quraysh, and chose him from Banu Hashim. Pupils draw a family tree: Abdullah, Aminah, Abdul Muttalib, Abu Talib. Link to Edexcel 1.1a. Exam tip: specify names and relationships, not just 'his family'.

teach.heading: Childhood influences
bullets: Halimah of Banu Sa'd nursed him in the desert
Mother Aminah died when he was about six
Grandfather Abdul Muttalib cared for him until he died, about two years later
Uncle Abu Talib then protected him
teach.note: Ask: what does his orphanhood teach about Allah's care? Quote 93:6 ('Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?'). Abu Talib protected him for decades but did not accept Islam. Be precise: do not claim details beyond the seerah.

teach.heading: Bahira and the journey to Sham
bullets: Aged about twelve, he travelled with Abu Talib's caravan to Syria
Bahira the monk noticed signs and advised protection
Reported by Ibn Ishaq and mentioned in Tirmidhi
Shows early signs of the Prophet's future role
teach.note: Present as a recorded event with some difference between scholars on the details. Edexcel names Bahira explicitly. Ask: why did Abu Talib take the young Muhammad on the trip? Warn against adding invented details; stick to the core facts (the monk's recognition of the signs and his advice to return).

teach.heading: Youth and character
bullets: Worked as a shepherd
Known as al-Amin, the trustworthy
Took part in the Hilf al-Fudul pact to defend the wronged
Did not worship idols
teach.note: Hilf al-Fudul: the Prophet later praised it (Ahmad). The Black Stone story shows wisdom in resolving disputes. Ask: how does being a shepherd prepare someone to lead? (Patience, care; Bukhari: every prophet shepherded sheep.)

teach.heading: Why does the early life matter?
bullets: He grew up honest and trusted
Hardship built patience and compassion
The Quraysh later could not deny his past
Allah prepared him to carry the message
teach.note: Edexcel 1.1b. Model a PEEL paragraph: Point (character), Evidence (al-Amin), Explanation (people trusted his word), Link (so when he called them to Allah they knew he did not lie). Pupils write the second paragraph.

practice: Name the Prophet's grandfather and the uncle who protected him.
State two events from the Prophet's early life.
Short-answer practice: 'State what the Prophet's work as a shepherd taught him' (2 marks).
independent: Write a timeline from the Year of the Elephant to age 25 with at least eight events.
Write a 6-mark style answer: 'Explain two ways in which the Prophet's early life prepared him for his mission.'
Draw the family tree and add one fact about each person.
exit: Who was Bahira and why is he important?
Give one way the early life prepared him for prophethood.
lessons.homework: Complete the 6-mark answer if unfinished; learn the names and relationships in the family tree.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-labelled timeline and sentence stems for PEEL; stretch: discuss why Edexcel asks about early influences.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The Prophet's early life and the Revelation (spec 1.1-1.2)
lessons.title: 1.1 Business, marriage to Khadijah, and family life (Qur'an 66:1-3)
objectives: Describe the Prophet's work and business before revelation
Explain his relationship with Khadijah and his children
Analyse Qur'an 66:1-3 and what it teaches about his family life

keywords.def: the Prophet's first wife, a respected Makkan businesswoman
Khadijah's servant who travelled with the Prophet
Mothers of the Believers: the Prophet's wives
trust

starter: Give two events from the Prophet's childhood.
What is the meaning of the word amanah?

teach.heading: A trusted trader
bullets: Khadijah hired him to trade for her in Syria
He travelled with her servant Maysarah
The trip brought great profit and honesty was noted
Business built trust with merchants
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.1: his work and business before revelation. Ask: what qualities does a successful trader need, and how does honesty help? Link to lesson on riba and honest trade in KS3.

teach.heading: Marriage to Khadijah
bullets: Married at about 25; Khadijah was a widow of good reputation
Their marriage lasted about 25 years
She supported him at the first revelation
He loved and remembered her all his life
teach.note: Khadijah's words after Hira (Bukhari) show her insight. Aisha said she never felt jealous of any wife as of Khadijah because of how often the Prophet mentioned her (Bukhari, Muslim). Keep factual. Ask: what does this teach about spouses?

teach.heading: Children and wives
bullets: Children with Khadijah: Qasim, Abdullah, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah
Ibrahim was born from Mariyah
After Khadijah he married several wives for reasons such as support and unity
He was gentle with his family
teach.note: Be sensitive and precise. Aisha reported that he used to help in the house and mend his clothes (Ahmad, graded sahih). Bukhari records his tenderness with his grandsons. Do not go deeper than the spec requires; teach respectfully and avoid polemics.

teach.heading: Qur'an 66:1-3
bullets: Allah addressed the Prophet about what he made unlawful for himself
Allah gave Muslims the way out of oaths
A confidence was shared and Allah informed him
Allah is the Knowing, the Acquainted
teach.note: The Edexcel passage. Scholars mention narrations about the occasion of revelation; the main lessons are agreed: the Prophet is accountable to Allah, revelation corrects and guides, and he is a human being in a household with real relationships. Ask: how does Allah's closeness appear here? Warn against over-detailed claims about the occasion.

teach.heading: Analysing the passage
bullets: What qualities of Allah appear? (Knowing, Wise, Acquainted)
What message is given about making lawful things unlawful?
How should believers reflect on this?
teach.note: Model annotating: underline Allah's attributes; note that no one has the right to forbid what Allah made lawful (also 5:87). Give pupils a 12-mark practice stem: 'Muslims should follow the Prophet's example in family life. Discuss.' Plan, don't write.

practice: List four members of the Prophet's family and their relationship to him.
Identify two attributes of Allah in 66:1-3.
Short answer: 'Explain why the Prophet's marriage to Khadijah was important' (4 marks).
independent: Annotate Qur'an 66:1-3 with attributes of Allah, lessons, and links to his family life.
Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two ways Khadijah supported the Prophet.'
Plan a 12-mark answer for the stem on following the Prophet's family example.
exit: What business did the Prophet do for Khadijah?
Name two attributes of Allah from 66:1-3.
lessons.homework: Write a 12-mark answer using your plan, including a different viewpoint.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: annotated passage with highlighted keywords; stretch: evaluate different interpretations of the occasion of revelation using the 'scholars differ' formula.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The Prophet's early life and the Revelation (spec 1.1-1.2)
lessons.title: 1.2 The Night of Power and the first revelation (Qur'an 97:1-5)
objectives: Describe the events in the cave of Hira in detail
Explain the importance of the Night of Decree
Analyse Qur'an 97:1-5

keywords.def: the Night of Decree/Power
revelation
the angel who conveyed revelation
Read/Recite: the first command revealed

starter: How did she help the Prophet?

teach.heading: Hira and the conversation with Jibril
bullets: He retreated to Hira in Ramadan to worship
Jibril said: 'Read!'
He replied: 'I am not a reader'
Jibril pressed him three times, then revealed 96:1-5
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Narrated by Aisha in Bukhari. Edexcel 1.2a: the details of the conversation. Learn the dialogue accurately. Ask: why does the response 'I am not a reader' matter? (He could not have authored it.)

teach.heading: Aftermath
bullets: He returned trembling to Khadijah: 'Cover me'
Khadijah comforted him and listed his good character
Waraqah ibn Nawfal confirmed this was the same angel who came to Musa
Revelation paused, then resumed
teach.note: Highlight Khadijah's reasoning from character. Waraqah's statement that he would be driven out shows the later opposition. Explain the 'pause' (fatrah) briefly: scholars differ on its length; it then resumed with Surah al-Muddaththir (74:1-2).

teach.heading: The Night of Decree
bullets: 'We sent it down on the Night of Decree' (97:1)
'Better than a thousand months' (97:3)
Angels and the Spirit descend (97:4)
'Peace it is until the rising of dawn' (97:5)
teach.note: Edexcel passage 97:1-5. Link to 2:185: the Qur'an began to be revealed in Ramadan. The Prophet ﷺ advised seeking it in the last ten nights (Bukhari, Muslim). The exact night is not fixed. Ask: what does 'better than a thousand months' tell us about worship on that night?

teach.heading: Why it was important
bullets: It marks the start of prophethood
It began the Qur'an's revelation
It started the message of Islam in Makkah
Muslims commemorate it by worship in Ramadan
teach.note: Exam tie: Edexcel asks for importance in the establishment of Islam. Model PEEL: 'The experience was important because it was the start of prophethood. The first words emphasised reading and knowledge. This shows Islam values learning. Therefore ...'

teach.heading: Analysis of 97:1-5
bullets: Who sent down the Qur'an? (Allah)
What is special about that night?
How do Muslims respond today?
What does 'Spirit' refer to? (Jibril)
teach.note: Annotate as a class. Model a 12-mark approach: reasons, views, conclusion. Stem: 'The Night of Power is the most important event in the history of Islam. Discuss.' Plan together.

practice: Write the conversation between Jibril and the Prophet in order.
State what Waraqah said.
Short answer: 'Explain why Laylat al-Qadr is important to Muslims' (4 marks).
independent: Annotate 97:1-5 and write three comprehension answers.
Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the experience in the cave of Hira was important.'
Plan the 12-mark question with two arguments for, two against, and a conclusion.
exit: What were the first words revealed?
How many months is the Night of Decree better than?
lessons.homework: Write up the 12-mark answer on the importance of the Night of Power.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: dialogue sequencing and vocabulary list; stretch: analyse the significance of 'Spirit' and 'by permission of their Lord'.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The Prophet's early life and the Revelation (spec 1.1-1.2)
lessons.title: 1.2 The importance of the revelation of the Qur'an
objectives: Explain the importance of the Qur'an to Muslims
Describe how revelation came to the Prophet
Evaluate the role of the Qur'an in Muslim life

keywords.def: the recitation: Allah's final revelation
the criterion between truth and falsehood
recitation
the inimitability of the Qur'an

starter: Why was the Night of Decree important?

teach.heading: Ways revelation came
bullets: True dreams
Jibril in the form of a man or in his true form
Sometimes like the ringing of a bell (Bukhari)
Direct revelation on certain occasions such as Isra and Mi'raj
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Harith ibn Hisham asked how revelation came and the Prophet ﷺ described a sound like a bell (Bukhari). Ask: why would Allah use different forms? The Qur'an came over about 23 years, in Makkah and Madinah.

teach.heading: Why the Qur'an matters
bullets: It is Allah's word and a guide for mankind (2:185)
It is the first source of Shari'ah
Recitation is worship and brings reward
It is preserved: 'We will guard it' (15:9)
teach.note: Use the Prophet's saying that whoever recites a letter of the Book of Allah gets a good deed, and each good deed is multiplied tenfold (Tirmidhi, hasan sahih). Ask pupils to rank reasons by importance and justify.

teach.heading: Gradual revelation
bullets: Revealed in stages over 23 years
Helped the Prophet and Companions stay firm (25:32)
Answered questions and events
Allowed gradual change in practice
teach.note: 25:32: 'that We may strengthen your heart thereby'. Example: the gradual prohibition of alcohol (2:219, 4:43, 5:90). Ask: why is gradual teaching effective?

teach.heading: A miracle that lasts
bullets: Linguistic excellence and challenge (2:23)
Unlettered Prophet brought it
Consistent over time and place
Many embraced Islam through hearing it
teach.note: Use 17:88 or 2:23 challenge: produce a surah like it. Mention Umar's conversion story as recorded in the seerah (note it has different versions). Ask: why might hearing the Qur'an move people regardless of background?

teach.heading: The Qur'an in Muslim life
bullets: Recited in daily prayers
Memorised by huffaz
Guides ethics, law and worship
Read and studied for understanding
teach.note: Exam link: 'importance of the Qur'an to Muslims' can come as a 6-mark: two reasons developed. Model: Reason 1: guidance (2:185). Development: it gives rules for life ... Reason 2: worship ... Write jointly.

practice: Name two ways revelation came to the Prophet.
Explain why the Qur'an was revealed gradually.
Short answer: 'State two ways Muslims show respect to the Qur'an' (2 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Qur'an is important to Muslims.'
Make a mind map of the Qur'an's roles in daily life.
Plan a 12-mark answer: 'The Qur'an is the most important source of guidance for Muslims. Discuss.'
exit: Give two reasons for the gradual revelation.
Which verse says Allah will guard the Qur'an?
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer, including the Sunnah as another source and a conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: reasons cards to sort; stretch: compare how different Muslims engage with the Qur'an.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The Prophet's early life and the Revelation (spec 1.1-1.2)
lessons.title: 1.2 How the Qur'an was compiled
objectives: Describe how the Qur'an was recorded in the Prophet's lifetime
Explain the compilation under Abu Bakr and Uthman
Evaluate the importance of the compilation

keywords.def: scribes of revelation
one who has memorised the whole Qur'an
the compiled written Qur'an
the battle in 11-12 AH in which many reciters were killed

teach.heading: In the Prophet's lifetime
bullets: Revelation was memorised and recited in prayer
Scribes wrote it on bones, leather and palm leaves
Zayd ibn Thabit and others served as scribes
Jibril reviewed the Qur'an with the Prophet each Ramadan
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Mention that Jibril reviewed it with him twice in his final year (Bukhari). Edexcel 1.2c. Ask: why combine memory and writing?

teach.heading: Abu Bakr's compilation
bullets: Many reciters were killed at Yamamah
Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the Qur'an
Zayd ibn Thabit collected it carefully from written pieces and memorisers
The pages were kept by Abu Bakr, then Umar, then Hafsah
teach.note: From Bukhari (Zayd ibn Thabit's narration). Zayd required two witnesses for each verse. Ask: why was Zayd chosen? (Young, intelligent, a scribe, and he heard the final review.)

teach.heading: Uthman's standard copies
bullets: Different recitations and dialects began to cause disputes
Uthman asked Hafsah for the pages
A committee copied the Qur'an in the Quraysh dialect
Copies were sent to major cities; other versions were collected
teach.note: Bukhari: Hudhayfah feared people would differ as earlier communities did. The committee included Zayd, Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As and Abd ar-Rahman ibn al-Harith. Pupils create a flow chart.

teach.heading: Why it matters
bullets: Protected the text from loss
Unified the community
Created a standard text still used today
Shows seriousness of the Companions
teach.note: Link to 15:9. Misconception: 'The Qur'an was written by Uthman.' Correct: Uthman unified copies; the content was from the Prophet. Evaluate: which stage was most important and why?

teach.heading: Exam skill: 6 marks
bullets: Explain two reasons with developed detail
Use specific names and events
Link back to the question
Aim for ~100 words
teach.note: Model: 'One reason ... was Yamamah. Many huffaz died. This showed the risk of losing the Qur'an if it depended only on memory. Therefore Abu Bakr ordered its compilation.' Pupils write the second reason.

practice: Put in order: Yamamah, Uthman's copies, scribes in Prophet's lifetime, Abu Bakr's compilation.
Why did Umar propose gathering the Qur'an?
Short answer: 'State two things Uthman did' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the compilation of the Qur'an was important.'
Create a flow chart showing the stages with names and dates.
Write a 150-word paragraph answering the misconception about Uthman.
exit: Who led the collection under Abu Bakr?
Why did Uthman copy the Qur'an?
lessons.homework: Prepare a revision card with the stages of compilation and key names.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing cards; stretch: evaluate the argument that the compilation under Uthman was the most important step.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - Prophethood and opposition (spec 1.3-1.4)
lessons.title: 1.3 The Prophethood of Muhammad and the Seal of the Prophets (Qur'an 33:38-40)
objectives: Explain the meaning of Seal of the Prophets
Explain the importance of Muhammad's role as prophet
Analyse Qur'an 33:38-40

keywords.def: Seal of the Prophets: the last prophet
the message and messengership
conveying the message
the Muslim community

starter: How did Khadijah react to the first revelation?

teach.heading: The passage
bullets: Those who convey Allah's messages fear Him alone (33:39)
Allah is sufficient as Accountant
Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and last of the prophets (33:40)
Allah is Knowing of all things
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel passage 33:38-40. Annotate. Explain that 33:38 says there is no blame on the Prophet regarding what Allah made obligatory on him. Ask: what do the verses say about the courage of the prophets?

teach.heading: What does 'Seal' mean?
bullets: The last of the prophets; no prophet after him
Hadith of the brick: the final brick in a completed building (Bukhari, Muslim)
'There is no prophet after me' (Bukhari, Muslim)
His revelation is complete and preserved
teach.note: Explain the building analogy narrated by Abu Hurayrah: the Prophet said he is the missing brick and the seal of prophets. Misconception: claims of new prophets contradict this verse and hadith; ahl as-sunnah regard it as consensus. Keep language calm and factual.

teach.heading: His role in establishing Islam
bullets: Conveyed the Qur'an
Explained it by word and example
Built the first Muslim community
Showed how to practise worship and character
teach.note: Edexcel 1.3b. Ask pupils to give an example for each: Qur'an (recitation), explanation (how to pray), community (Madinah), character (al-Amin). Link to 33:21.

teach.heading: Universal message
bullets: 'We sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds' (21:107)
'To all mankind as a bringer of good news and warner' (34:28)
Earlier prophets were sent to their peoples
teach.note: Compare: Musa to Bani Isra'il, Muhammad to all humanity; the hadith of five things given (Bukhari, Muslim, Jabir). Ask why finality requires universality and preservation.

teach.heading: Importance for Muslims today
bullets: Love and obey him
Follow his Sunnah
Send blessings on him
Defend his honour with good character
teach.note: Hand out the 12-mark stem: 'The most important thing about Muhammad is that he was the last prophet. Discuss.' Plan: for (completes revelation), against (example, leadership), conclusion.

practice: Explain 'Seal of the Prophets' in one sentence.
Find two ideas about Allah in 33:38-40.
Short answer: 'Explain why Muslims believe Muhammad was the last prophet' (4 marks).
independent: Write the 12-mark answer using your plan with a conclusion.
Create a diagram showing the role of Muhammad in establishing Islam.
Annotate 33:38-40 with the meaning of each phrase.
exit: What is the meaning of khatam an-nabiyyin?
Give two verses that show the universality of his message.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the role of Muhammad as prophet was important in establishing Islam.'
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: annotate with colours; stretch: evaluate whether finality implies the Qur'an is complete guidance.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - Prophethood and opposition (spec 1.3-1.4)
lessons.title: 1.3 Opposition faced in Makkah
objectives: Explain the reasons for Quraysh opposition
Describe forms of opposition faced by the Prophet and his followers
Evaluate how the Muslims responded

keywords.def: the period of ignorance before Islam
inviting to Islam
refusing to deal with a group
a fierce Makkan leader opposed to Islam

starter: Give one reason the message was universal.

teach.heading: Why did Quraysh oppose?
bullets: Threat to idol worship and pilgrimage income
Challenge to tribal pride and leadership
Message of equality and accountability
Fear of losing status
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.3c. Ask pupils to rank reasons by importance. Emphasise that opponents did not deny his honesty; they feared the change.

teach.heading: Forms of opposition
bullets: Mockery and accusations (poet, sorcerer, madman)
Offers of wealth and leadership
Physical abuse of weak Muslims
Pressure on Abu Talib to stop him
teach.note: Mention the accusation that a human taught him (16:103) and the Qur'anic response. The offer of wealth and kingship is in the seerah (Ibn Ishaq). The Prophet's reply 'If they place the sun in my right hand ...' is reported in the seerah with differing chains; summarise instead of quoting.

teach.heading: Treatment of the Muslims
bullets: Bilal tortured on hot sand
Sumayyah and Yasir killed
Khabbab was tormented
Some migrated to Abyssinia
teach.note: Handle with sensitivity. Khabbab's complaint and the Prophet's answer (Bukhari) show resilience. Abyssinia: two migrations; the Negus gave protection; Ja'far recited Surah Maryam (Ahmad).

teach.heading: The Prophet's response
bullets: Patience and steadfastness
Continued to preach
Sought protection of Abu Talib
Turned to Ta'if and was rejected
teach.note: Ta'if: Aisha's hadith (Bukhari, Muslim) of the angel of the mountains and the Prophet's reply: he hoped Allah would bring from their descendants those who worship Allah alone. Ask: what does this show about his character?

teach.heading: Exam link
bullets: Explain opposition with specific examples
Show the effect on early Muslims
Evaluate how it shaped the Muslim community
teach.note: Practice 6-mark response and discuss 12-mark stem: 'Opposition in Makkah made the Muslim community stronger. Discuss.' Plan together.

practice: Give three reasons why Quraysh opposed Islam.
Describe how Bilal was treated.
Short answer: 'State two forms of opposition faced by the Prophet' (2 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Quraysh opposed the Prophet.'
Plan and begin the 12-mark answer on whether opposition strengthened the community.
Create a table of opposition types, people affected, and response.
exit: Name two Companions who were persecuted.
How did the Prophet react at Ta'if?
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer with a conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: causes and effects table; stretch: evaluate to what extent the opposition was religious versus economic.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - Prophethood and opposition (spec 1.3-1.4)
lessons.title: 1.4 The boycott, the Year of Sorrow and the Mi'raj
objectives: Describe the boycott and its effects
Explain the events of the Mi'raj
Evaluate the significance of the Mi'raj for the Muslim community

keywords.def: the social and economic ban on Banu Hashim and Banu Muttalib
the valley where the boycotted families stayed
the night journey
the ascension

starter: Name two forms of opposition in Makkah.
Which Companion was tortured on hot sand?

teach.heading: The boycott
bullets: The Quraysh wrote a document to isolate Banu Hashim
No marriage, trade or contact
It lasted about three years in the valley of Abu Talib
Hunger and hardship tested the Muslims
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.4a. The boycott began around the seventh year of prophethood. It ended when some Quraysh men opposed the injustice. Ask: why did Banu Hashim including non-Muslims stay with the Prophet? (Tribal loyalty.)

teach.heading: The Year of Sorrow
bullets: Abu Talib died
Khadijah died soon after
Quraysh persecution increased
The Prophet went to Ta'if
teach.note: Explain the personal and political loss: his protection and his closest supporter. Ask: how might you feel? Emphasise his reliance on Allah. Link to the Ta'if du'a (seerah).

teach.heading: The Isra and Mi'raj
bullets: Night journey to al-Aqsa (17:1)
Ascension through the heavens
Meeting earlier prophets
Salah was prescribed: five prayers
teach.note: Bukhari and Muslim narrations (Anas, Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah). Allah comforted His Messenger with honour. The reduction from fifty to five prayers is a mercy. Date: scholars differ on the exact year; place it in the later Makkan period.

teach.heading: Reactions and significance
bullets: Quraysh mocked him; Abu Bakr affirmed it
Tested the faith of believers
Gave Muslims the gift of salah
Linked al-Masjid al-Haram with al-Aqsa
teach.note: Edexcel: the importance of the Mi'raj. Ask: how does this event connect Muhammad with earlier prophets? Develop PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link.

teach.heading: Exam practice
bullets: Short answer: state two effects of the boycott
6 marks: explain two reasons Mi'raj was important
12 marks: evaluate the claim that the Mi'raj was the most important event in Makkah
teach.note: Model the 12-mark plan: arguments for (salah, honour, comfort), arguments against (revelation, Hijrah), judgement. Remind pupils to use evidence.

practice: List the effects of the boycott on the Muslims.
Explain why the Year of Sorrow was difficult.

The second pledge was made by 73 men and two women
They promised to protect him as they protect their families
Mus'ab ibn Umayr taught them the Qur'an

They planned to kill him using one man from each clan

Ali slept in his bed; the Prophet left at night

Asma brought food; Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr brought news
A guide, Abdullah ibn Urayqit, led them
'Do not grieve; Allah is with us' (9:40)

He asked for safety and gave up the chase
The Prophet promised him a future reward
They reached Quba and then Madinah

the Prophet's mosque in Madinah
the emigrants from Makkah

He first stayed in Quba and built its mosque
Then he entered Madinah on his camel
Each family hoped to host him; he stayed where the camel knelt
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Bukhari reports the joy: the people greeted him with 'Allahu akbar'. Ask: why did the Prophet leave the choice to the camel? (To avoid favouring any clan.)

Masjid an-Nabawi built on land purchased from two orphans
Muslims worked together, including the Prophet
It served as a place of prayer, learning, consultation and care

teach.heading: Brotherhood and new society

Sharing of homes and wealth
Agreement among communities in Madinah
Market and justice established

teach.heading: The Hijrah hadith

'Whoever migrated for worldly gain or marriage, his migration is for that'
teach.note: Edexcel passage for 1.4. Annotate: the hadith was said in connection with a migration, and teaches intention and sincerity. Ask: how does the hadith shape the meaning of Hijrah beyond geography?

teach.heading: Significance of the Hijrah
bullets: Start of the Islamic calendar
Allowed Muslims to practise freely
Created the first Muslim state/community
Turning point from persecution to growth

keywords.def: the truthful: title of Abu Bakr
the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood: title of Umar
possessor of two lights: title of Uthman
the Rightly Guided Caliphs

starter: Name the mosque built at Quba.

teach.heading: Abu Bakr
bullets: First adult free man to accept Islam
Freed enslaved Muslims such as Bilal
Companion in the cave and the Hijrah
Spent his wealth for Islam
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Qur'an 9:40 calls him 'the second of two'. Bukhari: the Prophet said that if he were to take an intimate friend (khalil) other than his Lord, he would have taken Abu Bakr. Ask: which acts show loyalty?

teach.heading: Umar
bullets: Accepted Islam in Makkah and strengthened the Muslims
Known for justice and courage
Advised the compilation of the Qur'an
Became the second caliph
teach.note: The Prophet said Satan avoids any path Umar takes (Bukhari, Muslim). After Umar's conversion, the Muslims prayed more openly at the Ka'bah (reported by Ibn Mas'ud in Bukhari).

teach.heading: Uthman
bullets: Migrated to Abyssinia and Madinah
Married two of the Prophet's daughters (Ruqayyah then Umm Kulthum)
Funded the Tabuk expedition and bought the well of Rumah
Standardised the Qur'an
teach.note: The well of Rumah and Tabuk funding are in the sources (Bukhari, Tirmidhi). Ask: what does his generosity teach about using wealth?

teach.heading: Ali
bullets: One of the first to accept Islam as a youth
Slept in the Prophet's bed on the night of the Hijrah
Brave in battles such as Khaybar
Fourth caliph and a learned Companion
teach.note: The flag at Khaybar hadith (Bukhari, Muslim: Sahl ibn Sa'd). Ask pupils to compare the four with one trait each. Avoid sectarian debate; teach the positions of ahl as-sunnah respectfully: love and honour all the Companions.

teach.heading: The Ansar
bullets: Gave refuge and help to the Muhajirun
Defended the Prophet in battle
Praised in the Qur'an (59:9; 9:100)
'Love of the Ansar is a sign of faith' (Bukhari, Muslim)

Short answers, then a 6-mark explanation
Then a 12-mark question based on a passage
Use your own or others' views in the 12-mark

About 90-120 words

Explain how it supports your point

lessons.title: 1.5 The Sunnah: what it is and why it matters (Qur'an 33:36)
lessons.bigQuestion: If the Qur'an is the word of Allah, why would Muslims also need the words and actions of the Prophet ﷺ?
objectives: To understand what the Sunnah is and why it has authority for Muslims alongside the Qur'an
successCriteria: All: define Sunnah and hadith and the three forms of Sunnah
Most: explain the set passage 33:36
Some: use 33:21, 4:80 and 59:7 to explain the authority of the Sunnah
lessons.crossCurricular: History: primary sources and their reliability
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: following the Prophet ﷺ as an act of love and obedience

keywords.def: the way of the Prophet ﷺ: his sayings, deeds and approvals
a report recording what he said, did or approved
saying, action, silent approval
an excellent example (33:21)
the right to be obeyed and followed

hook.text: If the Qur'an is the word of Allah, why would Muslims also need the words and actions of the Prophet ﷺ?
hook.a: The Qur'an itself commands following him (33:36, 4:80); the Sunnah explains and applies the Qur'an.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair' (al-Ahzab 33:36). This is the set passage for 1.5.

starter.q: Which set passage goes with 1.4?
Who slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed on the night of the Hijrah?
Which ayah calls him the Seal of the Prophets?
In which year CE was the Hijrah?

teach.heading: What is the Sunnah?
bullets: The Prophet's ﷺ whole way of life
Hadith: the report that carries it
Qur'an: Allah's words; Sunnah explains and applies them
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. In fiqh 'sunnah' can also mean a recommended act; the specification uses it for his whole way.

teach.heading: Three forms
teach.note: Pupils need one example of each in exam answers.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: How he prayed: 'Pray as you have seen me pray' (Bukhari)
Companions' actions he saw and allowed

teach.heading: Set passage: 33:36 and its support
bullets: 33:36: no choice once Allah and His Messenger decide
33:21: an excellent example
4:80: obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah
59:7: take what the Messenger gives you
teach.note: Read 33:36 slowly. 'No choice' means a believer does not set aside a clear ruling; questions to understand are still welcome. Teacher checks the Arabic in a mushaf if displayed.

check.q: What does 33:36 teach about the Sunnah?
options: Believers follow what Allah and His Messenger decide
Only the Qur'an must be followed
check.why: 33:36 joins Allah and His Messenger: a clear decision of the Messenger is binding. The other options contradict the ayah.

teach.heading: Why it matters today
bullets: Shows how to perform worship
A model of character for every role
Unites Muslims in practice
Protects against misreading the Qur'an
teach.note: 12-mark statement: 'Muslims today need the Qur'an but do not need the Sunnah.' Some argue the Qur'an alone is enough; reply from the Qur'an itself (4:80, 16:44, 59:7) and from practice (salah, zakah, Hajj details).

practice.q: Explain two reasons why the Sunnah is important to Muslims.
practice.a: 1) It explains the Qur'an in practice, e.g. salah (16:44). 2) It has authority: obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah (4:80; 33:36). Each developed.
practice.model: I do reason 1: 'Point: the Sunnah shows how to follow the Qur'an. Evidence: the Qur'an commands prayer, and the Prophet ﷺ said "Pray as you have seen me pray" (Bukhari). Explain: without the Sunnah, Muslims would not know the movements or number of rak'ahs. Link: so the Sunnah is essential to worship.'

practice.q: A Companion did something in front of the Prophet ﷺ and he stayed silent. Which form?

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a set-passage answer: 'Explain what Qur'an 33:36 teaches Muslims about the Sunnah.' Refer to the passage directly.
independent.a: Quotes or paraphrases 33:36; explains that the Messenger's decisions are binding; links to 4:80, 33:21; gives a practical example.
independent.model: Teacher models the opening: 'Qur'an 33:36 says that when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, believers have no choice. This teaches that ...'

independent.q: Extend: sort ten statements (pupil PDF) into qawl, fi'l and taqrir.
independent.a: As in the answer key on the pupil PDF.

independent.q: Stretch: write the opening of a 12-mark answer to 'Muslims today need the Qur'an but do not need the Sunnah', giving the view of someone who agrees.
independent.a: Some argue the Qur'an is complete and preserved; Sunnah reports vary in strength. Then turn to the counter.

exit.q: Which ayah calls the Prophet ﷺ an excellent example?
Back to our ponder: why do Muslims need the Sunnah?
exit.a: The Qur'an commands following him, and the Sunnah explains and applies the Qur'an.

lessons.homework: Learn 33:36 and its meaning; write one example each of qawl, fi'l and taqrir.

lessons.title: 1.5 How the Sunnah was recorded and its role in belief and practice
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we be confident a saying from 1,400 years ago is accurate?
objectives: To understand how the Sunnah was recorded and checked, and its role in Muslim belief and practice
successCriteria: All: describe how the Sunnah was memorised, written and collected
Most: explain isnad, matn and the grades of hadith
Some: explain the Sunnah's role in belief and practice, including Shia and Sunni collections
lessons.crossCurricular: History: evaluating the reliability of sources
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the Muslim tradition of scholarship

keywords.def: the chain of narrators
the words of the report
authentic
weak
the six main Sunni hadith collections

hook.text: How can we be confident a saying from 1,400 years ago is accurate?
hook.a: Chains of trusted narrators (isnad), memory and writing, grading by scholars, and the great collections.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We revealed to you the Reminder so that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them' (an-Nahl 16:44).

starter.q: Which set passage goes with 1.5?
Taqrir means ...
Which ayah: 'obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah'?
Name the three forms of Sunnah.

teach.heading: Preserving the Sunnah
bullets: Memory: Companions learnt and repeated
Practice: the community lived it daily
Writing: e.g. Abdullah ibn Amr
Collection: scholars gathered books
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Abu Dawud reports Abdullah ibn Amr writing with permission. Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ telling Companions to write a sermon for Abu Shah after the conquest of Makkah.

teach.heading: Checking reports
bullets: Isnad: who told whom, back to the Prophet ﷺ
Matn: the words, checked against the Qur'an
Narrators checked for honesty and accuracy
Grades: sahih, hasan, da'if
teach.note: Ibn al-Mubarak: 'The isnad is part of the religion' (introduction to Sahih Muslim). The warning 'whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire' (Bukhari and Muslim) explains the care taken.

check.q: What is the isnad of a hadith?
check.why: Isnad is the chain; the matn is the words; the grade is the scholars' judgement of reliability.

teach.heading: The collections
teach.note: Keep it factual and respectful. Shia Muslims revere the Sunnah and use their own major collections (for example al-Kafi), accepting narrations especially through the family of the Prophet ﷺ; the difference lies in which narrators and chains are accepted.

left.title: Sunni collections
points: Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah

right.title: Shia collections
points: Narrations through the Imams of the Prophet's ﷺ family

teach.heading: Role in belief and practice
bullets: Practice: salah, zakah amounts, Hajj rites
Belief: details of the unseen and the Hereafter
Character: a model for every role
Law: a source of Shari'ah after the Qur'an
teach.note: Ask: what would Hajj look like with no Sunnah? The Prophet ﷺ said 'take your rites from me' (Muslim).

practice.q: Describe how the Sunnah was preserved.
practice.a: Memorised and practised by the Companions, written by some (Abdullah ibn Amr), passed on with chains, checked and gathered into collections such as Bukhari and Muslim.
practice.model: I do: 'Describe' means give the features with detail: 'First, the Companions memorised his words and lived them daily. Second, some wrote them down, for example Abdullah ibn Amr ...'

practice.q: Which collection is regarded by Sunnis as the most authentic after the Qur'an?

independent.q: In the portal response box: 'Explain the role of the Sunnah in Muslim practice.' Give two developed points with examples.
independent.a: Points: shows how to worship (salah, Hajj); gives details of zakah; model of character; source of law. Examples and evidence (16:44; 'pray as you have seen me pray').
independent.model: Teacher models point 1: 'Point: the Sunnah shows Muslims how to carry out worship. Evidence: the Qur'an commands Hajj, but the Prophet ﷺ said "take your rites from me" (Muslim). Explain: ...'

independent.q: Extend: why did scholars check the matn as well as the isnad?
independent.a: A good-looking chain could still carry an error; the text must agree with the Qur'an and stronger reports.

independent.q: Stretch: explain one similarity and one difference in how Sunni and Shia Muslims use hadith.
independent.a: Similarity: both revere the Sunnah as a source. Difference: they accept different chains and collections.

exit.q: Which grade means authentic?
Back to our ponder: how can we be confident?
exit.a: Chains, checked narrators, memory and writing, grading and collections.

lessons.send: SEND: chain diagram to label. EAL: glossary. Stretch: research the conditions of a sahih hadith.

lessons.title: 1.6 Social and economic justice in the Prophet's ﷺ teaching and example
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a society fair if its laws are good but the powerful can escape them?
objectives: To understand the Prophet's ﷺ teaching and example on social and economic justice
successCriteria: All: define 'adl and zulm with Qur'anic evidence
Most: describe two examples of social and two of economic justice
Some: explain what these show about Muslim beliefs about society
lessons.crossCurricular: Business (4BS1 option): ethical business, fair wages and honest trading
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice for the weak and equality before the law

keywords.def: justice: giving everyone their right
oppression, injustice
obligatory giving to those in need
interest or usury, forbidden in Islam
rights

hook.text: Is a society fair if its laws are good but the powerful can escape them?
hook.a: No: the Prophet ﷺ warned that nations were destroyed for punishing the weak and sparing the noble (Bukhari and Muslim).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, stand firmly for justice as witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves, your parents and your relatives' (an-Nisa 4:135), and 'Allah commands justice and excellence' (an-Nahl 16:90).

starter.q: Name the two most authentic Sunni collections.
Isnad means ...
Which ayah is the 1.5 set passage?
What is zakah?
starter.a: Obligatory giving of 2.5% of savings above the nisab

teach.heading: What is justice?
bullets: 'Adl: giving every person their due
Stand for justice even against yourselves (4:135)
Be just even with those you dislike (5:8)
Messengers were sent so people uphold justice (57:25)
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Ask: is fairness the same as treating everyone identically? Teacher checks the ayat in a mushaf before display.

teach.heading: Equality before the law
teach.note: The hadith of the Makhzumi woman (Bukhari and Muslim). Read from a trusted translation and annotate: who is protected, who is warned, what principle is set.

quote.text: Those before you were destroyed because when a noble person stole they left him, and when a weak person stole they punished him. By Allah, if Fatimah the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand.

teach.heading: Economic justice
bullets: Wealth must not circulate only among the rich (59:7)
Zakah: the poor's right in wealth (9:60)
Riba forbidden; trade permitted (2:275)
Honest weights: woe to those who give short measure (83:1-3)
teach.note: Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead.

check.q: Which teaching is about ECONOMIC justice?
options: Wealth must not circulate only among the rich (59:7)
The noble and weak face the same law
Be just to those you dislike (5:8)
check.why: 59:7 is about the flow of wealth. The others are about justice in law and relationships.

teach.heading: Care for the weak
bullets: Orphans: do not oppress them (93:9)
Workers: 'they are your brothers' (Bukhari and Muslim)
Pay the worker his wage promptly (Ibn Majah)
Oppression is darkness on the Day of Judgement
teach.note: The hadith 'your servants are your brothers' (Abu Dharr) is in Bukhari and Muslim; 'oppression will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection' is in Bukhari and Muslim. The hadith on paying wages before the sweat dries is reported by Ibn Majah.

practice.q: Explain how the Prophet's ﷺ example promoted justice in society.
practice.a: 1) Same law for all: the Makhzumi woman. 2) Wealth for the poor: zakah and the ban on riba. Each with explanation and link to Muslim belief about society.
practice.model: I do point 1: 'Point: he applied the law equally to everyone. Evidence: he refused to excuse a noble woman of Makhzum and said even Fatimah would face the same law (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain: no one is above the law, which builds trust and fairness. Link: Muslims believe a just society protects the weak.'

practice.q: Which ayah says 'Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba'?

Seek knowledge and take part in society

teach.note: SENSITIVE: teach accurately and calmly. Banu Qurayzah broke their agreement during the siege (Trench, 5 AH); the judgement was given by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their chosen arbiter, according to their own law (Torah) as many Sira sources state; scholars discuss the sources. Present as a political and military matter of treason, not a religious judgement on Jews, and reject any use of the event to justify hatred. Teachers should pre-read and keep this factual. bullets: Wash hands, mouth and nose
Face, arms to the elbows
Wipe the head, wash ears and feet
Qur'an 5:6; ghusl and tayammum when needed
teach.note: Qur'an 5:6 describes wudu: face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, feet. Many scholars add the details of hands, mouth and nose from the Sunnah. Mention tayammum when no water. Schools differ on what breaks wudu; here give the common points (using the toilet, sleep, passing wind). Exam note: Shia wudu involves wiping the feet instead of washing, based on their reading of 5:6; the Academy teaches washing the feet, as Ahl al-Sunnah hold from the authentic Sunnah.

teach.heading: Times and direction
bullets: Prayer times are set by the sun
Face the Ka'bah in Makkah (Qur'an 2:144)
The qiblah unites Muslims worldwide
Travel and missed prayers have concessions
teach.note: 2:144 'turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque' secure; check wording. Note: the Prophet ﷺ first faced Jerusalem before the change in Madinah. For missed prayers: Bukhari 597 (pray when remembered; verify). For travel: shortening is allowed (4:101); neutral on duration since schools differ.

teach.heading: The movements and words
bullets: Takbir 'Allahu akbar' (الله أكبر)
Standing: recite al-Fatihah and a short surah
Ruku', then standing, then two sujud with a sitting between
Tashahhud and salam: السلام عليكم ورحمة الله
teach.note: Be careful to describe the common core. Words: Subhana Rabbiyal 'Adhim in ruku'; Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah; Subhana Rabbiyal A'la in sujud. A rak'ah is one cycle. Note that some schools place the hands differently and some say 'amin' aloud (and Shia Muslims may keep arms at the sides or use a clay tablet for the forehead); teach neutrally as 'differences of practice' and avoid ranking. Bows in ruku', saying words of glorification.
Stands up, then goes into sujud, forehead on the ground.
Sits briefly, performs a second sujud, and rises.

the sermon before Jummah
congregation
prayer leader
shortening prayer when travelling

teach.heading: Home or mosque?
bullets: Prayer may be offered at home alone
Prayer in congregation carries extra reward (Bukhari 645, Muslim 650)
The mosque is a centre for learning and community
Men are strongly encouraged to attend; women may pray at home or at the mosque
teach.note: The reward of congregation (27 degrees) is reported in Bukhari 645 and Muslim 650; verify. Note differences: many scholars regard congregation as obligatory for men and others as strongly recommended; Hanafis and others differ on women. Present neutrally. In Britain many mosques provide space for women. Ask: what are the benefits of praying together?

teach.heading: Qur'an 62:9-11
bullets: When called to Friday prayer, hasten to the remembrance of Allah ﷻ
Leave off business
After the prayer, disperse and seek Allah's bounty
Do not abandon the khutbah for trade or amusement
teach.note: 62:9 يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَاةِ مِن يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَذَرُوا الْبَيْعَ. Teacher to verify the Arabic. 62:11 speaks of people leaving the Prophet ﷺ standing in the khutbah when a caravan arrived. Ask: what balance between work and worship does the passage give? (Stop for the prayer, then return to work.)

teach.heading: Jummah
bullets: Two parts: khutbah then two rak'ahs
Held at midday on Friday, replacing Dhuhr
Obligatory for adult men; women may attend
Teaches the community, gives reminders and unity
teach.note: Describe the day: ghusl, clean clothes, early arrival, khutbah in two parts, two rak'ahs led by the imam. Mention that British workplaces and schools may accommodate Jummah; many pupils will have experience. Exemptions: women, travellers, sick people, children (not required).

teach.heading: Exemptions and concessions
bullets: Sick: pray sitting or lying (Bukhari 1117)
Travellers may shorten and combine (4:101)
Menstruation and postnatal bleeding: no prayer and no make-up
Children below puberty and those who lose capacity are not obliged
teach.note: Bukhari 1117: pray standing, if not able sit, if not able on your side (verify). Women's exemption is well known; note that prayer missed during menses is not made up (Aisha's report; verify). Safeguarding: be matter-of-fact and age-appropriate; invite questions privately. Combining prayers: Hanafi and Shia approaches differ from others; teach the concession neutrally.

Against: the Prophet ﷺ taught that the earth was made a place of prayer, so prayer is valid anywhere.
Judgement: both are valid; mosque prayer is especially valued but home prayer is essential for daily flexibility.

teach.heading: What fasting is
bullets: Abstaining from food, drink and marital relations from dawn to sunset
Intention (niyyah) is required
Suhur before dawn, iftar at sunset
Ramadan lasts 29 or 30 days, set by the moon
teach.note: Bismillah. Explain: a Muslim fasts from true dawn (fajr) until sunset (maghrib). Suhur is encouraged ('in suhur is blessing': Bukhari 1923, Muslim 1095; verify). Breaking the fast with dates and water is a Sunnah. Ramadan begins with moon sighting or calculation; communities sometimes differ; keep neutral.

teach.heading: Qur'an 2:183-185
bullets: Fasting was prescribed to earlier nations too
The aim: that you may attain taqwa
Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down
Allah ﷻ intends ease, not hardship
teach.note: 2:183 يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ. Teacher to verify. 2:185: 'Allah ﷻ intends ease for you and does not intend hardship'. Ask: how do ease and discipline go together? Annotate the three ideas: purpose (taqwa), connection to Qur'an, concession (ease).

teach.heading: Purposes and benefits
bullets: Taqwa and self-control
Empathy with the poor
Closer relationship with the Qur'an
Forgiveness: Bukhari 38 for fasting with faith and hope of reward
teach.note: The hadith 'Whoever fasts Ramadan with faith and seeking reward will have past sins forgiven' (Bukhari 38, Muslim 760; verify). Also Bukhari 1903: if one does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah ﷻ has no need for him giving up food and drink (verify). The point: fasting is more than hunger. Ask: what would a good fast look like in a school day?

teach.heading: Laylat al-Qadr today

Some do i'tikaf in the last ten nights
Seek forgiveness
Many give extra charity

bullets: The third pillar of Islam

Nisab is commonly linked to the value of 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver (teacher to confirm current figures with a reliable source or local mosque). Note that scholars differ on which standard to use and on some categories of wealth. Mathematics link: 2.5% of £4,000 is £100.

teach.heading: Purpose and significance

Purification: Qur'an 9:103
Community care: rich and poor linked
Obedience: it is a duty to Allah ﷻ

teach.heading: Abu Bakr and the first compilation
teach.note: After the Battle of Yamamah (about 11-12 AH, verify) many Qur'an reciters were killed. Umar feared parts could be lost and urged Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr asked Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written for the Prophet, to collect the Qur'an from written material and from memory, checking with witnesses. Abu Bakr kept the sheets; later they went to Umar, and then to his daughter Hafsa, a wife of the Prophet. Present it as a careful process, not an editing process.

hook.text: What would you need to know about someone's life before you trusted them with a message from God?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And He found you lost and guided you, and found you in need and made you self-sufficient' (ad-Duha 93:6-8).

teach.heading: Youth, work and character
bullets: Shepherd, then trader
Known as al-Amin, the trustworthy
Joined Hilf al-Fudul to protect the wronged
Settled the Black Stone dispute at 35
teach.note: Hilf al-Fudul: a pact of Makkan clans to help anyone wronged; he later said he would still answer such a call in Islam (reported in the seerah). Black Stone: he placed it on a cloak so every clan lifted it together.

teach.heading: Khadijah and family life
bullets: Traded Khadijah's goods to Syria honestly
She proposed marriage; he was 25
Children: Qasim, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, Abdullah
A home of love and support

check.q: How did the Prophet ﷺ solve the dispute over the Black Stone?
options: He placed it on a cloak so every clan lifted it
He placed it alone without asking
He delayed it for a year
check.why: Every clan shared the honour, which prevented fighting. This showed wisdom and fairness, part of why he was trusted.

teach.heading: Set passage: Qur'an 66:1-3
bullets: 66:1: why forbid yourself what Allah made lawful?
66:2: Allah has given a way to release oaths
66:3: a private matter told to one wife was shared
teach.note: Read the set passage from a trusted translation. Teach the spec focus: the Prophet ﷺ was human, with a real family; Allah guided him in family matters too; trust and confidentiality in marriage matter. Keep the tone respectful; avoid speculation about details.

practice.q: Explain how ONE event from his early life prepared him to be trusted with the message.
practice.a: For example: the Black Stone: his fair solution showed wisdom and trust, so people knew he was honest and fair before he brought the message.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: the Black Stone dispute showed he was trusted. Evidence: at 35 every clan accepted his plan of lifting it together on a cloak. Explain: Quraysh already saw him as fair and honest (al-Amin), so his later claim to be a prophet came from someone with a spotless record.'

practice.q: At what age did he marry Khadijah, as commonly reported?
Which set passage is linked to 1.1?

independent.q: Timeline and explain (pupil PDF): place eight events from birth to marriage, then in the portal response box explain two ways his early life prepared him for prophethood.
independent.a: Accurate timeline; two developed explanations (orphanhood and trust in Allah, 93:6-8; honesty in trade; Hilf al-Fudul and justice; Black Stone and wisdom).
independent.model: Teacher places the first three events and models the first explanation: 'Being an orphan taught him to depend on Allah and to care for the weak (93:6-9).'

independent.q: Extend: what does 66:1-3 show about the Prophet's ﷺ family life?
independent.a: He was human with a real family; Allah guided him; trust in marriage matters.

independent.q: Stretch: why might Allah have chosen someone with a known honest record?
independent.a: So people could not accuse him of lying; his character was a proof of his truthfulness.

exit.q: Who cared for him after his grandfather died?
Back to our ponder: what made him trustworthy?
exit.a: His record: honesty in trade, fairness, keeping trusts, known as al-Amin.

hook.text: Why might the very first word revealed to the Prophet ﷺ have been 'Read'?
hook.a: Islam is a religion of knowledge; revelation begins with reading 'in the name of your Lord' (96:1).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, We sent it down in the Night of Power. And what will make you know what the Night of Power is? The Night of Power is better than a thousand months' (al-Qadr 97:1-3).

teach.heading: The first revelation (610 CE)
bullets: Aged 40, in retreat at Hira in Ramadan
Jibril: 'Read!' 'I am not one who reads'
Squeezed three times; then 96:1-5
Returned trembling: 'Cover me'
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. The account is in Bukhari (the third hadith, from Aisha) and Muslim. Ask: why was he afraid? It was overwhelming and new.

teach.heading: Khadijah and Waraqah
bullets: Khadijah: 'Allah will never disgrace you'
Because you keep family ties, help the weak, honour guests
Waraqah: the same angel who came to Musa
Revelation paused, then resumed (74:1-5)
teach.note: Khadijah's words list his good character (Bukhari). Waraqah called Jibril 'the Namus' who came to Musa and said his people would drive him out.

teach.heading: Set passage: Qur'an 97:1-5
teach.note: Annotate each ayah: what it says, what it shows. Pupils should be able to quote and explain the main ideas.

head: Ayah
Meaning
What it shows
rows: We sent it down in the Night of Power
A night of mercy and peace

teach.heading: From revelation to mushaf
bullets: Revealed over about 23 years
Memorised and written by scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit
Abu Bakr: gathered into one copy after Yamamah
Uthman: standard copies sent to the cities
teach.note: Both compilations are reported in Bukhari. Umar urged Abu Bakr after many huffadh died at Yamamah; Zayd ibn Thabit led the work. Uthman had copies made in the Quraysh dialect and sent to the main cities.

check.q: Why did Abu Bakr gather the Qur'an into one copy?
options: Many who had memorised it died at Yamamah
The Prophet ﷺ had never had it written
check.why: The loss of huffadh at Yamamah worried Umar and Abu Bakr. It had been written in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime; Uthman came later.

practice.q: Explain what 97:3 teaches about the Night of Power.
practice.a: It is better than a thousand months: worship on that night is worth more than a lifetime of nights, so Muslims seek it in the last ten nights of Ramadan.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: 97:3 says the Night of Power is better than a thousand months. Explain: a thousand months is over 83 years, so worship that night is worth more than a lifetime. Link: this is why Muslims seek it in the last ten nights of Ramadan.'

practice.q: What were the first words revealed?
practice.a: Iqra: 'Read in the name of your Lord' (96:1-5)

practice.q: Who led the compilation for Abu Bakr?

independent.q: In the portal response box, annotate the set passage 97:1-5 (meaning of each ayah) and then write a paragraph: 'Explain why the first revelation was important in establishing Islam.'
independent.a: Annotations as in the table; paragraph: beginning of the Qur'an and prophethood, the message of reading in Allah's name, Khadijah the first believer, start of 23 years of guidance.
independent.model: Teacher annotates 97:1 with the class: 'We sent it down: "We" is Allah; "it" is the Qur'an; so the Qur'an's source is Allah, revealed on a special night.'

independent.q: Extend: why is Uthman's compilation important today?
independent.a: It ensured one standard text in every city; the mushaf used today follows it.

independent.q: Stretch: what does Khadijah's reply show about the link between character and prophethood?
independent.a: His good deeds and character showed he was not someone Allah would disgrace; character supported the truth of his message.

exit.q: Which surah is the set passage for 1.2?
Back to our ponder: why 'Read'?
exit.a: Islam begins with knowledge, read in the name of Allah.

keywords.def: the Seal of the Prophets: the last prophet
the message and mission of a messenger
calling people to Islam
cruel treatment because of beliefs
the Christian kingdom where Muslims found refuge

hook.text: Why might powerful people oppose a message that calls for justice and the worship of One God?
hook.a: It threatened their idols, trade from pilgrims, tribal pride and power over the weak.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets, and Allah has full knowledge of all things' (al-Ahzab 33:40).

starter.q: Which set passage goes with 1.2?
Who said 'Allah will never disgrace you'?
Who standardised copies of the Qur'an?
In which year CE was the first revelation?

teach.heading: Set passage: Qur'an 33:38-40
bullets: 38: no blame for doing what Allah ordained
39: messengers convey and fear only Allah
40: Messenger of Allah and Seal of the Prophets
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Bridge lesson: fast-teach of 1.3. Read from a trusted translation. 'Seal' means the last: no prophet after him, and his message is complete and for all people (34:28).

teach.heading: From private to public call
bullets: About three years of private da'wah
First believers: Khadijah, Abu Bakr, Ali, Zayd
Public call on Mount Safa (26:214)
Abu Lahab's rejection (Surah al-Masad)
teach.note: 26:214: 'warn your closest kindred.' Bukhari reports the call from Safa and Abu Lahab's response, after which Surah al-Masad (111) was revealed.

teach.heading: Kinds of opposition
teach.note: Bilal was tortured by Umayyah ibn Khalaf; Sumayyah was the first martyr in Islam. Quraysh pressured Abu Talib and offered wealth and status (seerah).

items: Torture of the weak: Bilal, Sumayyah, Yasir
Bribes: offers of wealth and power

teach.heading: Why oppose?
bullets: Tawhid threatened the idols
Pilgrim trade at the Ka'bah
Equality threatened tribal pride
Fear of losing power
teach.note: In 615 CE some Muslims migrated to Abyssinia, where the Negus protected them after Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited from Surah Maryam (seerah reports). This shows the scale of the persecution.

check.q: Which reason for opposition was ECONOMIC?
options: Losing trade from pilgrims to the idols
check.why: Pilgrims visiting the idols brought trade to Makkah. The others are religious or social reasons.

practice.q: Explain what 'Seal of the Prophets' means for Muslims.
practice.a: He is the final prophet; no prophet comes after him; his message is complete and for all people; Muslims reject claims of later prophets.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: Seal of the Prophets means the Prophet ﷺ is the last prophet. Evidence: 33:40. Explain: just as a seal closes a letter, prophethood is complete. Link: so Muslims follow his Sunnah until the end of time.'

practice.q: Who was the first martyr in Islam?
Which surah was revealed about Abu Lahab?

independent.q: In the portal response box: 'Explain two reasons why the Quraysh opposed the Prophet ﷺ.' Use Point, Evidence, Explain, Link for each.
independent.a: Two developed reasons (religious: idols and tawhid; economic: pilgrim trade; social: equality vs pride; political: power), each with an example (Abu Lahab, Bilal, bribes).
independent.model: Teacher models reason 1: 'Point: Quraysh opposed the message because tawhid threatened their idols. Evidence: ... Explain: ... Link: ...'

independent.q: Extend: why did some Muslims go to Abyssinia?
independent.a: To escape persecution; the Christian king, the Negus, was just and protected them.

independent.q: Stretch: what does 33:39 teach about how messengers face opposition?
independent.a: They convey the message and fear only Allah, not people.

exit.q: Which set passage goes with 1.3?
Back to our ponder: why did powerful people oppose the message?
exit.a: Threat to idols, trade, pride and power.

hook.text: What turns a hard decision to leave home into an act of worship?
hook.a: The intention: 'whoever's hijrah was for Allah and His Messenger, his hijrah is for Allah and His Messenger' (Bukhari and Muslim).

teach.heading: Set passage: the hadith on intention
teach.note: Narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab. Link to the Hijrah: the Companions left homes and wealth for Allah; their reward depended on intention.

quote.text: Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended. Whoever's hijrah was for Allah and His Messenger, his hijrah is for Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's hijrah was for worldly gain or a woman to marry, his hijrah is for what he migrated for.

teach.heading: Support for the Prophet ﷺ (1.4e, f)
bullets: Abu Bakr: companion in the cave (9:40), spent his wealth
Ali: slept in his bed, returned the trusts
Uthman: generous with wealth for the community
Umar: his Islam strengthened the Muslims; migrated openly
teach.note: Umar's open migration is reported in the seerah. The Ansar welcomed and shared with the Muhajirun (59:9). Pupils need examples for each person in 1.4.

check.q: Which Companion slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed on the night of the Hijrah?
check.why: Ali stayed behind and returned the trusts. Abu Bakr travelled with the Prophet ﷺ; Uthman and Umar supported in other ways.

teach.heading: Why the Hijrah mattered
bullets: Freedom to practise Islam openly
The first Muslim community and mosque
The Prophet ﷺ as leader of Madinah
Start of the Islamic calendar (1 AH)
teach.note: 12-mark statement for the unit: 'The Hijrah was the most important event in establishing Islam.' Assess this statement. Pupils should be able to argue for (community, state, calendar) and against (the first revelation; the conquest of Makkah).

practice.q: Explain the link between the hadith on intention and the Hijrah.
practice.a: The Companions migrated, leaving homes and wealth; the hadith teaches the reward depended on the intention: for Allah, or for worldly gain.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: the hadith shows the Hijrah's value depended on intention. Evidence: whoever's hijrah was for Allah and His Messenger ... Explain: two people could make the same journey with different rewards. Link: the Muhajirun are honoured because they migrated sincerely.'

practice.q: How many pledges of Aqabah were there?
Which ayah describes the plot to kill the Prophet ﷺ?

independent.q: 12-mark practice plan in the portal response box: 'The Hijrah was the most important event in establishing Islam.' Write one paragraph for, one against, and a one-line conclusion.
independent.a: For: community, state, mosque, calendar, freedom. Against: first revelation began Islam; conquest of Makkah; Hudaybiyyah. Conclusion with justification.
independent.model: Teacher models the 'for' paragraph start: 'Some would agree, because the Hijrah allowed Muslims to form the first community where they could practise freely. For example, the Prophet ﷺ built Masjid an-Nabawi ...'

independent.q: Extend: describe how the Ansar supported the Muhajirun.
independent.a: Shared homes, wealth and work in the brotherhood (mu'akhah); 59:9 praises them.

exit.q: Which Companion was with the Prophet ﷺ in the cave?
Back to our ponder: what makes leaving home an act of worship?
exit.a: The intention: doing it for Allah and His Messenger.

hook.text: What makes an argument convincing to someone who disagrees with you?
hook.a: Evidence, fair treatment of the other view, and a conclusion that follows from the reasons.

teach.heading: Set-passage answers
bullets: Quote or paraphrase the passage accurately
Explain what it means
Say what it shows Muslims believe
Link to practice today
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Model with 33:36: quote the key phrase, explain 'no choice', show belief in the Messenger's authority, link to following the Sunnah today.

teach.heading: Building a 12-mark answer
teach.note: The 12-mark question asks pupils to assess a statement: arguments for, arguments against, evidence and a justified conclusion. Use the school scheme's sample questions.
cycle: Weigh: which is stronger and why?

teach.heading: Model plan
teach.note: Talk through the plan aloud; pupils copy the structure, not the words.

model.problem: 'Muslims today need the Qur'an but do not need the Sunnah.' Assess this statement.
steps: For: the Qur'an is complete and protected (15:9); some hadith are weak
Against: the Qur'an commands obedience to the Messenger (33:36, 4:80, 59:7)
Against: salah, zakah and Hajj details come from the Sunnah (16:44)
Weigh: the 'for' view contradicts the Qur'an it relies on
Conclusion: disagree; the Qur'an itself makes the Sunnah necessary
model.answer: A balanced answer with evidence on both sides and a justified conclusion.

teach.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Only one side argued
Evidence named but not explained
Conclusion just repeats the introduction
Running out of time: plan for 2 minutes
teach.note: Share two anonymised sample paragraphs (teacher-written) and ask pupils to improve them.

check.q: Which is the strongest argument AGAINST the statement?
options: The Qur'an itself commands following the Messenger (4:80)
The Sunnah is older than the Qur'an
check.why: It uses the Qur'an's own words, so it answers the statement directly. The other options are untrue or weak.

practice.q: Write a set-passage answer: 'Explain what the hadith on the just (Muslim) teaches about justice.'
practice.a: The just are honoured by Allah; justice applies in judgements, families and any responsibility; so every Muslim with responsibility must be fair.
practice.model: I do: 'This hadith teaches that the just will be on pulpits of light with Allah, which shows that justice is greatly rewarded. It names three areas: judgements, families and anything a person is put in charge of. This means ...'

practice.q: In a 12-mark answer, what must the conclusion do?

independent.q: Write a full 12-mark answer in the portal response box (or a Forms long-answer question): 'The Prophet's ﷺ example on justice is the best guide for society today.' Assess this statement. Aim for 20 minutes' worth; finish at home if needed.
independent.a: For: equality before the law, zakah, ban on riba, care for workers and orphans, with evidence. Against: some argue modern laws and human rights frameworks are enough, or societies differ. Weighing and justified conclusion.
independent.model: Teacher writes the first two sentences: 'Many Muslims would agree with this statement, because the Prophet ﷺ applied the law equally to rich and poor. For example ...'

exit.q: Which collection reports the hadith on the just?
Back to our ponder: what makes an argument convincing?
exit.a: Evidence, fair counter-arguments and a justified conclusion.
